title: Anthropic launches Claude Ship beta: AI handles code review, fixes, and approvals end-to-end
excerpt: The most painful parts of the code merge process—back-and-forth review feedback, mysterious CI check failures, and recurring merge conflicts—are being handed ov
content_html:
The most painful parts of the code merge process—back-and-forth review feedback, mysterious CI check failures, and recurring merge conflicts—are being handed over wholesale to AI by Anthropic. According to a report yesterday by tech publication TechCrunch, the company has launched Claude Ship Beta, a suite of tools made up of AI agents that can automatically handle code review, fixes, approvals, and more—essentially putting the entire stretch of the development pipeline from "checking" to "sign-off" under the banner of agents.

The suite is made up of three components. Leading the charge, Code Review is already generally available and handles the first gate: code review; the other two are still in beta. Among them, PR Steward plays the role of a "cleanup steward," dealing specifically with failed CI checks, merge conflicts, and feedback raised by Code Review—after each code push, it also explains in the comments exactly what it changed and, if necessary, how to undo those changes, laying every step out in the open.

The component that truly puts approval authority in AI's hands is Claude Approvals. It can carry out approvals according to policies set by the development team, and those policies are stored directly as files in the code repository and can be written in natural language—no need to build a complex rules engine; just write the requirements as a paragraph. During approval, it weighs multiple signals, drawing on Code Review's findings and also incorporating information from classifiers developed in-house by the company.

Still, Anthropic remains clear-eyed and cautious about "letting AI approve code." Because the entire suite is still in beta, the company recommends that teams first run the approval feature in observation mode—meaning the AI only makes judgments and does not actually execute approvals, so teams can see whether its judgment is reliable. Teams can also choose to enable the feature in a single repository first and set a monthly spending cap, keeping the scope and cost of trial and error within controllable bounds. As AI goes from "writing code" all the way to "approving code for production," the last gate left in developers' hands is to watch it perform first and then decide whether to let it do the real thing.
